sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Skanda** ​(*skanda*) — ‌War, the ‌Divine Hosts ​· ‘The ​Attacker’ — ​a name ​of Kārttikeya, ​son of ‌Śiva — ​belongs to ​the Sanskrit ‌tradition, where ​it is ‌catalogued under ​the ‌domain "War, ​Commander". The ​name means ​"‘The Attacker’ ​— a ​name of ‌Kārttikeya, son ​of Śiva ‌(or of ​Agni), the ‌god of ​war who ‌leads the ​divine ‌hosts against ​the enemies ​of the ‌gods."[^1].

**Skanda** ‌is the ‌Hindu war-god: ​the ever-youthful ​general of ‌the devas’ ​hosts, born ​from the ‌combined fire ​of Śiva’s ​third eye ‌to ​destroy the ‌demon Tāraka. ​Tamil India ​knows him ​as Murugan, ​the eternally ‌beautiful mountain ‌lord of ​the six ‌abodes; the ​Sanskrit world ​as Kārttikeya, ‌son of ‌the Pleiades’ ‌fosterage.[^2]

‌PuniCodex records ​the canonical ‌scholarly spelling ​**Skanda** and ​serves its ​temple at ‌[its temple](https://punicodex.com/skanda/). ​The displayed ​form is ​ASCII-equivalent — ‌a description ​computed from ​the displayed ​form ‌itself. The ​plain ASCII ‌form *skanda* ​contains the ‌same letters: ​no recovered ‌diacritics or ‌special encoding ​is claimed. ​The work ​here is ​consistent citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, transliteration, canonical spelling, name variations, and evidence preservation.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in Devanagari ​as ​**स्कन्द**. Etymologically ​it ​means "‘The ​Attacker’ ‌— a ​name ​of Kārttikeya, ‌son of ​Śiva ‌(or of ​Agni), ‌the god ​of ​war who ​leads ​the divine ​hosts ‌against the ​enemies ‌of the ​gods."[^1].

‌The canonical ​spelling ‌**Skanda** matches ​the ‌conventional scholarly ​romanization. ​The plain ‌ASCII form ‌*skanda* ‌contains the ​same ​letters, so ‌no ​lost diacritics ​or ‌encoding transition ​is ​claimed. The ‌editorial ​work is ‌to ​fix one ​reviewed ​reference spelling, ​preserve ‌capitalization and ‌provenance, ​and keep ‌the ​original evidence ​visible. The ‌displayed ‌form is ‌ASCII-equivalent ‌— a ​description ‌computed from ​the ​displayed form ​itself.

‌The letter-by-letter ​transformation ​runs:

- **s** ​→ ‌**S** — ​Same, ​capitalized
- **k** ​→ ‌**k** — ​Same
- ‌**a** → ​**a** — ‌Same
- ​**n** → ‌**n** ‌— Same
- ​**d** ​→ **d** ​— ​Same

sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is **/ˈskʌndə/** ​— ​Sanskrit ​(IAST: Skanda).[^1]

‌Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

- ‌**Skan-** — ​The ‌cluster ​sk is ‌preserved; ​short ​a ​as in ​“cup”.
- ​**-da** ‌— The ​name ‌means ​“the Attacker”, ‌“the ​Leaper” ‌— ​a war-name, ‌not ​a ​birth-name.
- **-n-** ‌— ‌The ‌cluster ​sk is ​preserved ‌in ​every period ​of ‌the ​language; no ​sound ‌is ​lost ‌between the ​s ​and ​the k.

​For ‌the ‌modern speaker, ​the ‌closest ​approximation ​is: “SKUN-duh”

‌Kindred ‌and ‌historical forms ‌of ​the ‌name:

- ​**Form** — ​Kārttikeya
- ​**Form** ‌— Murugan
- ​**Form** ​— ​Subrahmaṇya
- **Kumāra** ‌— ​(all ​the ​same god)
- ‌**Tamil** ​— ‌Murukan

One ​god, ‌six ​names ‌per tradition ‌— ​born ​of six ​sparks ​from ‌the gods’ ‌outraged ​eyes.

sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Skanda** ​is the ‌Hindu ‌war-god: the ​ever-youthful ​general ​of the ​devas’ ​hosts, born ‌from ​the combined ​fire ‌of Śiva’s ​third ‌eye to ​destroy ‌the ​demon Tāraka. ​Tamil ​India knows ​him ​as Murugan, ‌the ​eternally beautiful ‌mountain ​lord of ‌the ​six ‌abodes; the ​Sanskrit ‌world as ​Kārttikeya, ​son of ‌the ‌Pleiades’ fosterage.[^1]

### ‌The ​Divine General

​Commander ‌of ​the gods’ ​armies ‌— the ​deva-senāpati ​— before ‌whom ​no asura ‌line ​holds.

### Born ​of ​the ​Third Eye

‌Six ‌sparks from ​the ‌gods’ wrath-eyes, ​fostered ​by the ‌Kṛttikā ‌— the ‌Pleiades ‌— ​as six ‌infants, ​fused into ​one.

### ​The Spear

‌Śakti, ​the lance ​his ​mother Umā ‌gave ​him ​— one ​throw ‌ended Tāraka, ​the ‌boon-armed demon.

### ​Lord ‌of the ​Six ‌Abodes

Murugan’s ‌six ​mountain ​shrines from ​Tirupparankunram ​to Palani ‌mark ‌his Tamil ​country.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated ‌with Skanda ​concentrates ​in ​a ​small ​set ‌of ​recurring attributes, ​each ‌a ​compressed ‌statement ​about ‌the ​name:[^1]

- **The ​Divine ​General** ​— ​Commander ‌of ​the ‌gods’ armies ​— ‌the ​deva-senāpati ‌— ​before ‌whom no ​asura ​line ‌holds.
- ‌**Born ‌of ​the ​Third Eye** ‌— ​Six ​sparks ‌from ​the ​gods’ ‌wrath-eyes, fostered ​by ‌the ​Kṛttikā ​— ​the ​Pleiades ‌— as ‌six ​infants, ‌fused ​into ​one.
- ‌**The ‌Spear** — ‌Śakti, ‌the ​lance ‌his ​mother ​Umā gave ​him ‌— ​one ​throw ​ended ‌Tāraka, ​the boon-armed ​demon.
- ​**Lord ‌of ​the ‌Six ​Abodes** ‌— Murugan’s ​six ‌mountain ‌shrines ​from ​Tirupparankunram ​to ​Palani mark ‌his ‌Tamil ​country.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The Skanda ​myth is the war-god’s ‌birth-saga: the gods, ‌unable to defeat Tāraka, ​whose boon made ​him unkillable except by ​a son of ​Śiva, contrived the god’s ​marriage to Pārvatī; ‌the child was born ​as fire from ​the third eye, fostered ‌by the Pleiades, ​and general of heaven ‌before he was ​a week old. The ‌Tamil Murugan traditions ​add the wooing of ​Vaḷḷi, the huntress, ​and the gnostic doctrine ​of the *Arupadaiveedu*, ​the six stations of ‌grace.[^1]

### The Birth ​of Fire (Kumāra ‌Cycle)

When Agni and ​the river Ganges ‌could not carry the ​god’s seed, they ‌left it in the ​reeds of the ‌Gangā’s bank; six infants ​were found there ​by the six Kṛttikā ‌nymphs, each nursing ‌one — until Pārvatī ‌gathered them into ​a single six-headed child. ​His first week ‌closed with the death ​of Tāraka, slain ​by the spear his ‌mother gave him.[^2]

### ​The Deva-Senāpati (Skanda Purāṇa)

​The great Purāṇa ‌bearing his name makes ​him general of ‌the gods’ hosts and ​husband of Devasenā ​— ‘the army of ​the gods’ — ​a marriage arranged before ‌his birth. His ‌camp is on the ​world’s margin; his ‌peacock mount, the demon ​Siṃhakeśin subdued, struts ​beneath his banner.

### Vaḷḷi ‌and Teyvāyāṉai (Murugan ‌Cycle)

The Tamil epics ‌tell how Murugan ‌wooed the huntress Vaḷḷi ​in the guise ‌of a tree-shade, and ​wed both her ​and Teyvāyāṉai, Indra’s daughter, ​in the great ‌marriage at Tiruchendur. ​The legend’s two wives ​read theologically: divine ​grace (Teyvāyāṉai) and the ‌soul’s own effort ​(Vaḷḷi) are both needed ​for union with ​the lord.

### The Sage-Child ‌(Subrahmaṇya Cycle)

As ​Subrahmaṇya — ‘the dear ‌one to the ​Brahmins’ — he is ‌the teacher-god, expounding ​the Vedas to his ‌own father Śiva ‌in the role of ​guru. The image ​flips the war-god into ​wisdom’s child, and ​fixes his southern temples ‌as places of ‌learning as much as ​of arms.
